title: Shampoo, jungle, bungalow and loot are all Indian words
body: English took shampoo from the Hindi champo, to press or massage. Jungle comes from jangal, bungalow from bangla, a house in the Bengal style, and loot from lut. Pyjamas, veranda, thug, bangle and chutney arrived the same way during the centuries of trade and colonial rule.
takeaway: Words travel with people. The Oxford English Dictionary lists hundreds of entries of Indian origin.
source: Oxford English Dictionary; Yule & Burnell, Hobson-Jobson (1886)
visual: a colonial-era bungalow with a wide veranda at the edge of a dense jungle, a ship's trunk open on the steps

title: A banana is a berry and a strawberry is not
body: To a botanist a berry is a fleshy fruit that grows from a single flower's ovary and carries its seeds inside. Bananas, grapes, tomatoes, aubergines and chillies all qualify. A strawberry grows from the swollen base of the flower, and its true fruits are the tiny pips on the outside.
takeaway: Everyday names and scientific categories were made for different purposes. Neither is wrong.
visual: a banana, a tomato and a bunch of grapes grouped together on a dark table with a single strawberry set apart

title: Carrots were purple before they were orange
body: Carrots were first farmed in Central Asia about a thousand years ago, and they were purple or yellow. Orange carrots became common only in the 1500s and 1600s, bred by Dutch growers. The story that they were created to honour William of Orange has no solid evidence behind it.
takeaway: Much of what looks natural in a vegetable market is the result of centuries of deliberate breeding.
visual: a bunch of carrots in deep purple, pale yellow, white and orange lying on a rough wooden market table

title: Snakes and ladders began as an Indian lesson in morality
body: The game was played in India for centuries under names such as Moksha Patam and Gyan Chaupar. Ladders stood for virtues like generosity and faith, snakes for vices like anger and greed, and the final square for liberation. It reached England in the 1890s with the moral labels removed.
takeaway: Old boards had more snakes than ladders, to teach that a good life is harder than a bad one.
source: Victoria and Albert Museum; Andrew Topsfield, The Indian Game of Snakes and Ladders (1985)
visual: an antique painted cloth game board with a grid of squares, long coiling snakes and slender ladders, cowrie shells beside it

title: Badminton took shape in Pune
body: British army officers stationed in Poona, now Pune, in the 1860s and 1870s added a net to an old shuttlecock game and wrote down rules. They took the game home, where it was played in 1873 at Badminton House, the Duke of Beaufort's estate, and took its name.
takeaway: For some years the sport was simply known as Poona.
visual: nineteenth-century players in white on a lawn hitting a feathered shuttlecock over a net, an Indian cantonment building behind

title: The marathon is 42.195 km because of a royal viewing box
body: Early Olympic marathons were about 40 km. For the 1908 London Games the route was set to start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box in the stadium, which came to 26 miles 385 yards. In 1921 that odd figure was made the official distance.
takeaway: Many exact-looking standards began as one event's convenience.
visual: an exhausted runner in 1908 kit entering a packed stadium, a canopied royal box overlooking the finish line

title: There has never been lead in a pencil
body: Around 1564 a deposit of pure graphite was found at Borrowdale in England. It marked sheep and paper so well that people took it for a kind of lead. In 1795 the Frenchman Nicolas-Jacques Conté mixed powdered graphite with clay, which is how pencils are still made.
takeaway: More clay makes a harder, paler pencil. That is what the H and B grades describe.
source: Henry Petroski, The Pencil: A History of Design and Circumstance (1990)
visual: a rough lump of shiny grey graphite beside a row of hand-cut wooden pencils on an old workbench

title: Purple was royal because it took 10,000 snails to make a gram
body: Tyrian purple, the dye of Roman emperors, came from a gland of murex sea snails. Around 10,000 of them were needed for a single gram, so it was worth more than gold. In 1856 an 18-year-old student, William Perkin, made the first synthetic purple dye by accident.
takeaway: Colours that were once a sign of rank became ordinary once chemistry could make them.
source: Royal Society of Chemistry; Science Museum, London
visual: a heap of spiny sea snail shells beside a clay vat of deep purple dye and a length of rich purple cloth

title: Denim and jeans are named after two European cities
body: Denim comes from serge de Nîmes, a sturdy cloth from the French city of Nîmes. Jeans comes from Gênes, the French name for Genoa in Italy, whose sailors wore trousers of a similar fabric. Riveted jeans were patented in the United States in 1873 by Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis.
takeaway: The rivets were added because miners kept tearing the pockets off their work trousers.
visual: a pair of worn blue work trousers with copper rivets draped over a wooden crate in a nineteenth-century mining camp

title: A kilogram of saffron takes about 150,000 flowers
body: Saffron is the dried stigma of a purple crocus. Each flower has only three, and they must be picked by hand in the few autumn weeks when the plant blooms. That labour makes it the most expensive spice in the world by weight.
takeaway: Iran grows most of the world's crop. In India it is grown around Pampore in Kashmir.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
visual: hands gently pulling three red threads from a purple crocus flower, a field of the flowers stretching behind
